AFG.culture: Afghan life centers on hospitality, green tea, and dishes like kabuli pulao, with poetry recitation and kite fighting beloved pastimes. Nowruz, the Persian new year, is celebrated widely, and Islam shapes daily rhythms.
AFG.history: For thousands of years Afghanistan sat on the Silk Road between India, Persia and China, drawing conquerors from Cyrus the Great to Alexander the Great. Genghis Khan's Mongols devastated it in the 1200s, and later it was the heartland of the Mughal Empire founded by Babur in the 1500s. Ahmad Shah Durrani united the Afghan tribes and founded the Durrani Empire in 1747, often seen as the birth of modern Afghanistan. In the 1800s it became a buffer state in the Great Game between Britain and Russia, and the British failed twice to subdue it. A communist coup in 1978 and the Soviet invasion of 1979 led to decades of war, Taliban rule, and foreign intervention that continues to shape the country today.
AFG.funFact: Miners in the Panjshir valley have mined lapis lazuli, the deep blue stone used in Tutankhamun's death mask, for over 6,000 years.

ARM.culture: Armenian culture revolves around family feasts of dolma and lavash flatbread, duduk flute music, and the world's oldest national church. Chess is practically a school subject, and the Armenian alphabet is a point of huge pride.
ARM.history: Armenia emerged around 600 BC in the highlands near Mount Ararat and became one of the very first kingdoms to adopt Christianity as a state religion, in 301 AD. Ancient neighbors like the Persians and Romans fought over it, and in 405 AD monk Mesrop Mashtots invented the unique Armenian alphabet to keep the nation's identity alive. Medieval Armenian kingdoms flourished until waves of invaders, including Seljuk Turks and later Mongols, carved the land up. Armenia fell under Ottoman and Russian rule, and in 1915 Armenians in the Ottoman Empire suffered mass killings during World War One. After a brief independence, Armenia joined the Soviet Union in 1920 and regained independence in 1991 when it collapsed.
ARM.funFact: Armenia adopted Christianity as its state religion more than a decade before the Roman Empire did, around 301 AD.

AZE.culture: Azerbaijani culture blends Persian and Turkic traditions with a love of mugham, a haunting classical music genre recognized by UNESCO. Saffron rice pilaf, kebabs and black tea from pear-shaped glasses are everyday staples, and fire imagery appears everywhere from temples to brand names.
AZE.history: The land of Azerbaijan, where natural gas seeps burned the ground for millennia, was ruled in turn by ancient Caucasian Albanians, Persian empires and Arab caliphs who brought Islam. The Silk Road city of Baku grew rich on oil and trade, and medieval dynasties like the Shirvanshahs left stunning architecture. Persian Safavids and Ottoman Turks wrestled over the region before Russia annexed it in the early 1800s. After a short-lived independent republic in 1918, Azerbaijan joined the USSR in 1920 and became a major oil supplier, then won independence in 1991 when the Soviet Union dissolved. Conflict with neighboring Armenia over Nagorno-Karabakh has marked its modern era.
AZE.funFact: Azerbaijan has hundreds of mud volcanoes, more than almost anywhere else on Earth, and some erupt with flames fed by natural gas.

BHR.culture: Bahraini culture grew from the sea: pearl diving songs, dhow boats and date palms define the Gulf island life. Majlis gatherings with coffee and dates are a core custom, and the kingdom is known as one of the more open societies of the Arabian Peninsula.
BHR.history: Bahrain Island was home to the ancient Dilmun civilization over 4,000 years ago, a legendary trading paradise between Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley. It later passed through Babylonian, Greek, Persian and Arab hands, and Islam arrived in the 600s when the Prophet Muhammad sent envoys to its rulers. Portuguese raiders seized it in the 1500s before Persian and then the Al Khalifa family took control in 1783, a dynasty that still reigns. Britain signed protection treaties in the 1800s, and Bahrain declared independence in 1971 as British influence withdrew from the Gulf. Oil discovered in 1932 made it the first Gulf state to find black gold, and it transformed into a modern financial hub.
BHR.funFact: A lone acacia tree called the Tree of Life has survived for around 400 years in the middle of the desert with no visible water source.

famous: the six-yard sari of Dhaka muslin
BGD.culture: Bangladeshi life follows the rhythms of its rivers: rice and fish, especially the beloved hilsa, are food staples, and boat races and Baul folk music fill festivals. The struggle to defend the Bengali language is celebrated every February as Language Martyrs' Day.
BGD.history: Bengal was a treasure of successive empires: Buddhist Pala kings ruled from the 700s, then Hindu Sena dynasties, before Muslim sultans took over in the 1200s. The Mughal Empire made Dhaka a capital of fabulously rich muslin trade in the 1600s, calling it the City of Mosques. The British East India Company seized control after the Battle of Plassey in 1757 and colonial rule devastated the muslin industry. When British India was partitioned in 1947, Bengal became East Pakistan, ruled from faraway Karachi despite deep differences of language and culture. Resentment exploded in 1971 when Pakistan's army cracked down on Bengali nationalists, and after a brutal nine-month war with Indian support, Bangladesh won independence.
BGD.funFact: Bangladesh's independence war in 1971 lasted only nine months but created a nation of over 170 million people, one of the most densely populated countries on Earth.

BTN.culture: Bhutanese life is steeped in Mahayana Buddhism: prayer flags flutter on ridgelines, masked dance festivals called tshechu fill fortress monasteries, and chili cheese stew called ema datshi is the beloved national dish. Everyone wears traditional gho robes and kira dresses in public.
BTN.history: For centuries Bhutan was a patch of valleys organized around Buddhist monasteries in the eastern Himalayas, shielded by mountains. In 1616 the Tibetan lama Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal unified the valleys into a single state under a system of religious and civil leaders. Bhutan fought border skirmishes with British India in the 1800s and signed a treaty in 1910 letting Britain guide its foreign affairs while staying independent. The monarchy began in 1907 when Ugyen Wangchuck was crowned the first king, and the Wangchuck dynasty still reigns. Bhutan deliberately modernized slowly, guarded its forests and culture, invented Gross National Happiness as its guiding philosophy, and held its first democratic elections in 2008 when the fourth king gave up absolute power.
BTN.funFact: Bhutan is the world's only carbon-negative country, its forests absorb more carbon than the whole nation produces.

BRN.culture: Bruneian culture is Malay and Islamic, with stilt villages called kampong ayer rising over the water and lavish royal ceremonies during Ramadan and Hari Raya. No alcohol is sold, and Friday prayers empty the streets as the whole country pauses.
BRN.history: The Brunei Sultanate rose around the 1400s and under Sultan Bolkiah became a powerful maritime empire controlling Borneo and parts of the Philippines at its height around 1500. Spanish and later British traders and colonizers chipped away at the empire until it shrank to its present sliver of Borneo. Brunei became a British protectorate in 1888 but kept its sultans, an unbroken Muslim dynasty since the 1400s. When Britain withdrew in 1984, Brunei became fully independent and one of the world's richest countries per person, thanks to offshore oil and gas. The current sultan, Hassanal Bolkiah, is one of the longest-reigning monarchs alive.
BRN.funFact: Brunei's royal family lives in the world's largest residential palace, Istana Nurul Iman, with nearly 1,800 rooms.

KHM.culture: Cambodian culture carries deep Khmer roots: amok fish curry steamed in banana leaves, graceful apsara dance from temple carvings, and water festivals on the great Tonle Sap lake. Monks in saffron robes are a daily sight, and Theravada Buddhism shapes family life.
KHM.history: The Khmer Empire rose around 802 AD when Jayavarman II declared himself a god-king, and for six centuries it dominated Southeast Asia. Its kings built Angkor, a city of a thousand temples including the colossal Angkor Wat, perhaps the largest religious monument ever built, fed by a vast irrigation network. The empire declined from the 1400s, squeezed by Siamese and Vietnamese neighbors, and Angkor was abandoned to the jungle. Cambodia became a French protectorate in 1863 to survive its neighbors, regaining independence under King Norodom Sihanouk in 1953. The horror came in 1975 when the Khmer Rouge under Pol Pot emptied the cities and killed around a quarter of the population; Vietnam toppled the regime in 1979, and Cambodia slowly rebuilt into the peaceful kingdom it is today.
KHM.funFact: Angkor was likely the largest pre-industrial city in the world, home to nearly a thousand people at a time when London had tens of thousands.

CHN.culture: Chinese culture spans dumplings and dim sum, calligraphy and brush painting, festivals like Lunar New Year with red envelopes and dragon dances. Confucian respect for education and family runs deep, and tea drinking is a ritual nearly 2,000 years old.
CHN.history: Chinese civilization began on the Yellow River with dynasties like the Shang around 1600 BC, and the first emperor Qin Shi Huang unified China in 221 BC, building the Great Wall's early form and an army of terracotta soldiers. Great dynasties followed: the Han opened the Silk Road, the Tang made Chang'an the world's most cosmopolitan city, and the Song invented printing, gunpowder and paper money. Mongol Kublai Khan ruled as the Yuan dynasty, then the Ming built Beijing's Forbidden City and sent treasure fleets across the seas, while the last dynasty, the Qing, ruled into the 1900s. Defeats by Western powers and Japan, the 1911 revolution that ended empire, and the civil war that brought Mao Zedong's Communist Party to power in 1949 transformed the country. Decades of upheaval, including the Cultural Revolution, gave way to reform and opening from 1978, turning China into the world's second-largest economy within a generation.
CHN.funFact: China's high-speed rail network is longer than the rest of the world's combined, with trains that zip between cities at over 300 kilometers per hour.

GEO.culture: Georgian culture revolves around the supra, a feast led by a toastmaster where endless toasts accompany khachapuri cheese bread and khinkali dumplings, all washed down with wine. Ancient polyphonic songs and the unique Georgian alphabet, one of the world's oldest still in use, define national pride.
GEO.history: Georgia's highlands between Europe and Asia were home to kingdoms like Colchis, home of the Golden Fleece in Greek myth, and Iberia, which adopted Christianity in the 300s AD. The golden age came under Queen Tamar in the 1100s and 1200s, when the medieval kingdom stretched across the Caucasus and produced the epic poem The Knight in the Panther's Skin. Mongols, Persians and Ottomans repeatedly ravaged the land before Russia annexed it in 1801 to shield it from its Muslim neighbors. Georgia declared independence in 1918 during the Russian collapse but was absorbed by the Soviet Union in 1921, and its son Joseph Stalin became the Soviet dictator. Independence returned in 1991, followed by wars with separatist regions and a 2008 war with Russia, while the country pushed toward Europe.
GEO.funFact: People in Georgia have made wine in clay pots called qvevri for about 8,000 years, the oldest known winemaking on Earth.

HKG.culture: Hong Kong blends Cantonese tradition with global speed: morning tea with dim sum carts, mountain trails minutes from glass towers, and festivals like the Cheung Chau bun carnival. Feng shui shapes even skyscrapers, which often have dragon-shaped gaps for spirits to pass through.
HKG.history: Hong Kong was a cluster of fishing villages on China's southern coast until the First Opium War, when Britain defeated Qing China and took Hong Kong Island in 1842, adding Kowloon in 1860 and the New Territories in 1898 on a 99-year lease. The port became a free-trade crossroads for opium, tea and silk, drawing merchants and refugees from across Asia. After 1949 waves of migrants fleeing mainland China fueled manufacturing, and by the 1980s Hong Kong was a neon-lit financial powerhouse under British rule. The lease expired and Britain handed the territory back to China in 1997 under the one country, two systems promise, keeping its own laws and freedoms for 50 years. Recent years have seen growing friction as Beijing has tightened control over the city.
HKG.funFact: Hong Kong has more skyscrapers than any other city on Earth, over 550 of them stacked between steep mountains and the sea.

IND.culture: Indian culture is a carnival of regional cuisines from fiery curries to street chaat, festivals like Diwali the festival of lights and Holi the festival of colors, and classical arts from Bharatanatyam dance to sitar music. Family, cricket and chai thread through everyday life across a dozen major faiths.
IND.history: India's story begins with the Indus Valley cities of Harappa and Mohenjo-daro over 4,000 years ago, followed by Aryan kingdoms, Buddhism's birth under the Buddha, and the vast Maurya Empire, whose emperor Ashoka renounced war around 260 BC. The Gupta era is called a golden age of mathematics, when the concept of zero was developed, and later Mughal emperors like Akbar and Shah Jahan, who built the Taj Mahal in the 1600s, ruled a wealth that drew European traders. The British East India Company took over piecemeal from the 1700s and the Crown made India the jewel of its empire, while figures like Gandhi led resistance through nonviolence. Independence in 1947 came with the painful Partition, which split off Pakistan and displaced millions. Modern India has become the world's most populous country and a spacefaring democracy of many languages.
IND.funFact: India invented the game of chess's ancestor chaturanga, and the digits we call Arabic numerals actually came from India.

IDN.culture: Indonesian culture spans hundreds of ethnic groups and languages, united by spice-laden dishes like nasi goreng and rendang, gamelan orchestras, and wayang shadow puppets. The national motto is Unity in Diversity, and batik cloth patterns carry meanings passed down for centuries.
IDN.history: Indonesia's islands grew rich on the spice trade, with Hindu-Buddhist kingdoms like Srivijaya and Majapahit ruling vast sea empires in the medieval era. Islam spread through Indian and Arab merchants from the 1200s, and the Dutch East India Company began seizing the spice monopoly in the 1600s, turning the islands into the Dutch East Indies. Japanese occupation during World War Two broke Dutch power, and Indonesia declared independence in 1945 under Sukarno, confirmed after a four-year struggle. Dictator Suharto ruled for three decades of growth and repression before falling in 1998, and Indonesia has since become a vibrant democracy. It now spans a volcanic arc from Sumatra to Papua, sitting on the Pacific Ring of Fire.
IDN.funFact: Indonesia stretches farther than the distance from London to Tehran, with over 17,000 islands of which only around half are inhabited.

IRN.culture: Iranian culture treasures poetry by Hafez and Rumi, saffron-rich dishes like tahchin, and Nowruz, the ancient spring new year with a table of seven symbolic items. The Persian language, tea houses, and intricate carpet weaving carry a civilization's memory forward.
IRN.history: Iran is heir to the Persian Empire founded by Cyrus the Great in 550 BC, which ruled from Egypt to India and famously freed the Jews of Babylon; his successor Darius built Persepolis and the world's first postal roads. Alexander the Great burned Persepolis in 330 BC, but Persian dynasties like the Parthians and Sassanians revived the empire and rivaled Rome for centuries. Arab armies brought Islam in the 600s, and Persia wove it into a distinct Shia culture under the Safavid dynasty, whose capital Isfahan was called half the world. Invasions by Mongols and Turks reshaped the land, and the Qajar and Pahlavi dynasties ruled into the 1900s as Britain and Russia competed for influence. The 1979 Islamic Revolution toppled the Shah and created the Islamic Republic, which has defined Iran's confrontations with the West ever since.
IRN.funFact: The Persian Empire's Royal Road let a message travel nearly 2,700 kilometers in a week, inspiring the saying that neither snow nor rain stops the couriers.

IRQ.culture: Iraqi culture feeds on the twin rivers: Masgouf grilled fish by the Tigris, poetry recitation in Baghdad's tea houses, and maqam music with roots over a thousand years old. Family gatherings around rice dishes like quzi and celebrations of Eid carry both Arab and Kurdish traditions.
IRQ.history: Iraq is ancient Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates where Sumerians invented writing around 3200 BC, and where Babylon's Hammurabi wrote one of the first law codes nearly 4,000 years ago. It later sat at the heart of Assyrian, Babylonian and Persian empires before the Arab conquest of 636 AD made it the core of the Islamic world. The Abbasid caliphs founded Baghdad in 762 AD, and its House of Wisdom gathered the planet's scholars to translate and advance science and philosophy. Mongols destroyed Baghdad in 1258, and after centuries of Ottoman rule Britain created modern Iraq from three former provinces in 1920. A 1958 revolution ended the monarchy, Saddam Hussein seized power in 1979, and his wars with Iran, the invasion of Kuwait, and the 2003 US-led invasion led to decades of turmoil and a fragile democracy rebuilding from the ruins.
IRQ.funFact: Iraqis have been brewing beer-like drinks and writing literature for over 4,000 years, and the world's first author known by name was a Mesopotamian princess, Enheduanna.

ISR.culture: Israeli culture mixes Jewish traditions from around the world with Middle Eastern flavors: hummus and falafel debates, klezmer and Mizrahi music, and Shabbat dinners that gather families every Friday. The country is one of the world's most science-focused societies.
ISR.history: Ancient Israelite kingdoms rose here around 1000 BC under kings David and Solomon, and Jerusalem became a spiritual center that outlasted conquest by Assyrians, Babylonians, Persians and Romans, who destroyed the Second Temple in 70 AD and scattered the Jews. The land then passed through Byzantine, Arab, Crusader and Ottoman rule for nearly two millennia. Persecution in Europe fueled the Zionist movement, and after the Holocaust Britain's Mandate ended and Israel declared independence in 1948, immediately attacked by Arab neighbors. Wars in 1948, 1967 and 1973 redrew borders and left unresolved conflicts with Palestinians and neighboring states that continue today. Despite this, Israel built a high-tech economy and has made peace with several Arab countries in recent years.
ISR.funFact: The Dead Sea shore is the lowest dry land on Earth, and it is sinking by about a meter every year.

JPN.culture: Japanese culture balances ancient ritual and neon modernity: tea ceremony and cherry blossom viewing alongside anime, arcade districts and bullet trains. Meals like sushi, ramen and kaiseki are treated as art, and politeness, festivals and craftsmanship shape daily life.
JPN.history: Japan was shaped by imperial courts and borrowed Chinese culture, then fell under warrior rule when the first shogun took power in 1192. Daimyo warlords fought for a century until three unifiers, Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu, reunified the country, and the Tokugawa shogunate sealed Japan off from the world for over 200 years of peace, the Edo period. US ships forced the country open in 1853, and the Meiji Restoration of 1868 put the emperor back at the head of a mad dash to industrialize. Imperial Japan won wars against China and Russia, then embarked on conquest through Asia and the Pacific until surrendering in 1945 after atomic bombs fell on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Under US occupation Japan adopted a pacifist constitution, then astonished the world by becoming an economic superpower within a few decades.
JPN.funFact: Japan is made of around 14,000 islands and has more than 5 million vending machines, one for roughly every 23 people.

JOR.culture: Jordanian culture is built on hospitality: mansaf, the lamb and yogurt rice dish, is served at every celebration, and the black iris is the national flower. Bedouin traditions of coffee, poetry and desert camps remain a living part of national identity.
JOR.history: Jordan's deserts and trade routes hosted ancient kingdoms like the Nabataeans, who carved the rose-red city of Petra into cliffs and grew rich on frankincense caravans before Rome annexed it in 106 AD. The land later passed through Byzantine, Umayyad, Ottoman and other Muslim empires, dotted with crusader castles and desert palaces. After World War One the Ottoman Empire collapsed, and Britain created the Emirate of Transjordan in 1921 under Abdullah of the Hashemite family, descendants of the Prophet Muhammad. The emirate became fully independent in 1946 and fought in the wars surrounding Israel's creation, absorbing waves of Palestinian refugees. Under King Hussein and now King Abdullah II, Jordan has stayed a rare island of stability in a turbulent region despite hosting millions of refugees.
JOR.funFact: Petra was lost to the Western world for centuries until Swiss explorer Johann Burckhardt rediscovered it in 1812 by tricking his guides into taking him to it.

KAZ.culture: Kazakh culture carries nomad DNA: yurts, eagle hunting, dombra music and horse dishes like beshbarmak, with tea poured only half-full to show the host is attentive. Nauryz spring festival brings the whole steppe together.
KAZ.history: The Kazakh steppe was crossed by Scythians and Silk Road caravans before Genghis Khan's Mongols swept through in the 1200s. Kazakh tribes coalesced in the 1400s under the Kazakh Khanate, living as legendary nomadic horsemen until the Russian Empire gradually absorbed the steppe in the 1700s and 1800s. Soviet rule collectivized nomads with devastating famines in the 1930s, and Kazakhstan became the USSR's rocket launch site, nuclear test ground and gulag destination. Independence came in 1991 when the Soviet Union collapsed, the last Soviet republic to leave. Nursultan Nazarbayev ruled for nearly three decades, and oil wealth turned Kazakhstan into Central Asia's richest country, now rebranding itself with a new alphabet and capital.
KAZ.funFact: Every human sent to space by the Soviet Union and Russia, including Yuri Gagarin, launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.

KWT.culture: Kuwaiti culture blends seafaring and desert roots: pearl diving songs, machboos spiced rice with fish or lamb, and the diwaniya, a nightly majlis gathering where men debate everything from football to politics. The souks and the corniche along the Gulf anchor city life.
KWT.history: Kuwait grew in the 1700s when the Al Sabah family and merchant clans founded a port town that thrived on pearling and trade between Iraq, India and Arabia. The Ottoman Empire claimed loose authority until Britain signed a protectorate agreement in 1899, and oil discovered in 1938 transformed a poor pearl fishery into one of the richest states on Earth. Kuwait gained independence in 1961 and built the Arab world's first constitution and parliament. In 1990 Saddam Hussein's Iraq invaded and annexed Kuwait, looting the country, until a US-led coalition drove the Iraqis out in the Gulf War of 1991. Since then Kuwait has remained a stable, oil-rich emirate with one of the region's most active parliaments.
KWT.funFact: Kuwaiti singers once worked the pearling season to exhaustion, and their sea shanties called fijiri are considered the soul of Kuwaiti music.

KGZ.culture: Kyrgyz culture is proudly nomadic: yurt camps in alpine meadows, epic poetry reciters who can perform the 500,000-line Manas epic, and kok-boru horseback games. Kumis, fermented mare's milk, is the traditional drink of the summer pastures.
KGZ.history: The mountains of Kyrgyzstan were crossed by Silk Road caravans and ruled in turn by Turkic khaganates, Karakhanids, and the Mongol Empire. The Kyrgyz people consolidated in the Yenisei region and Tien Shan, and the epic hero Manas became the symbol of their struggle to stay free. The region fell under the Kokand Khanate before Russia annexed it in the 1800s, and Soviet rule brought cotton farming, industry and a written Cyrillic script. Independence came suddenly in 1991 with the Soviet collapse, and Kyrgyzstan earned the nickname Switzerland of Central Asia for its mountains and its relatively open politics. Two revolutions, in 2005 and 2010, made it the most turbulent yet most democratic state in the region.
KGZ.funFact: Lake Issyk-Kul, the world's second-largest high mountain lake, never freezes despite its name meaning hot lake.

LAO.culture: Lao culture flows with the Mekong: sticky rice eaten by hand, alms-giving to orange-robed monks at dawn, and the gentle Lao lam folk music. Theravada Buddhism and French colonial touches mix in riverside towns like Luang Prabang.
LAO.history: Ancient Laos was home to mysterious jar-burial sites like the Plain of Jars, iron age fields dotted with giant stone vessels. The Kingdom of Lan Xang, the Land of a Million Elephants, was founded in 1353 by Fa Ngum and dominated the Mekong valley for over three centuries before splitting into rival kingdoms. Burma, Siam and Vietnam competed for control, and Siam eventually dominated until France made Laos a protectorate in 1893, adding it to French Indochina. Laos became independent in 1953, but was then dragged into the Vietnam War era as a CIA secret war and massive bombing campaign ravaged the countryside. The communist Pathet Lao took power in 1975, and Laos remains one of the world's few socialist states, slowly opening its jungle-covered, river-carved land to tourism.
LAO.funFact: Laos is the most heavily bombed country per person in history; unexploded bombs from the 1960s and 70s are still being cleared today.

LBN.culture: Lebanese culture is famous for mezze feasts of hummus, tabbouleh and kibbeh, fairuz ballads on every balcony, and cafes where debates never end. Mountain villages, beach clubs and ski slopes sit within an hour of each other.
LBN.history: Lebanon's coast was home to the Phoenicians, the master sailors who invented the alphabet and founded trading posts across the Mediterranean over 3,000 years ago. Its legendary cedar forests supplied Egypt and Babylon, and the land later passed through Assyrian, Persian, Roman, Arab, Crusader and Ottoman rule. After World War One France took the region and carved out Greater Lebanon in 1920, blending Muslim and Christian communities, and independence came in 1943 with a delicate power-sharing pact between religions. Beirut became the Paris of the Middle East until civil war tore the country apart from 1975 to 1990, drawing in Syrian and Israeli forces. Lebanon has since rebuilt and struggled through repeated crises, but its resilience and cultural flair endure.
LBN.funFact: The word Bible comes from Byblos, a Lebanese port city that has been continuously inhabited for about 7,000 years.

MYS.culture: Malaysian culture is a Malay, Chinese and Indian blend: nasi lemak breakfasts, roti canai stalls, Deepavali lamps next to Ramadan bazaars and Chinese New Year lion dances. Batik, kampung village life and a passion for badminton round out daily life.
MYS.history: The Malacca Sultanate, founded around 1400, turned the strait between the Indian and Pacific Oceans into the world's spice crossroads and made Malay the region's trading language. Portuguese seized Malacca in 1511, the Dutch pushed them out in 1641, and Britain took over in the 1800s, drawing Chinese and Indian laborers to tin mines and rubber plantations. Japan occupied Malaya in World War Two, and after the war Britain united its colonies into Malaya, which became independent in 1957. Malaysia formed in 1963 by joining with Singapore and Borneo states, though Singapore was expelled after two tense years in 1965. The country industrialized rapidly, building the Petronas Towers, the world's tallest buildings at the turn of the millennium.
MYS.funFact: The Petronas Towers are joined by a double-decker skybridge built slightly apart from the towers so they can sway independently in high winds.

famous: some of the lowest land on Earth
MDV.culture: Maldivian culture mixes South Asian, Arab and African seafaring roots: bodu beru drumming, tuna in every form, and Islamic festivals marking the calendar. Life on tiny islands means the sea is pantry, highway and playground at once.
MDV.history: The Maldives were settled by sailors from India and Sri Lanka over 2,500 years ago, and Buddhist kingdoms left ruins before Arab traders brought Islam in 1153. The sultanate navigated the age of exploration, repelling Portuguese invaders in the 1500s and fending off later Portuguese and Malabari attacks. A British protectorate from 1887 left the sultans in charge of the islands, and the Maldives became fully independent in 1965, ending the monarchy in 1968 for a republic. Tourism from the 1970s transformed scattered fishing atolls into a luxury destination, and the nation now faces an existential battle against rising seas. Its former president famously held an underwater cabinet meeting in 2009 to highlight climate change.
MDV.funFact: The Maldives is the flattest country on Earth, and its highest natural point is only about 2.4 meters above sea level.

MNG.culture: Mongolian culture is nomadic: gers, the round felt tents, throat singing and the horsehead fiddle, dairy foods like airag and dried aaruul, and Naadam festivals of wrestling, archery and horse racing. Hospitality to strangers crossing the steppe is a sacred custom.
MNG.history: In 1206 the warlord Temujin united Mongolia's feuding tribes and became Genghis Khan, launching the largest land empire in history, which stretched from Korea to Hungary within decades of his death. His heirs ruled China as the Yuan dynasty and Persia as the Ilkhanate, and the Mongol peace opened the Silk Road wider than ever before. The empire fragmented, and Mongolia later fell under Buddhist theocracy, with reincarnate lamas ruling under Qing China's dominance from the 1600s. With Russian backing, Mongolia declared independence in 1911, became a Soviet satellite after 1924, and endured purges while herders were forced into collectives. Democracy arrived in 1990 with peaceful protests, and today Genghis Khan is celebrated as the father of the nation, his face on currency and mountainsides.
MNG.funFact: Genghis Khan's empire once connected so much of the world that legend claims an armored virgin could walk from Mongolia to Europe without fear, thanks to the Pax Mongolica.

famous: longyi skirts and thanaka face paint
MMR.culture: Burmese culture centers on merit-making: offering alms to monks, covering pagodas with gold leaf, and festivals like Thingyan, the water-splashing new year. Tea leaf salad is a beloved dish, and everyone wears the longyi sarong with thanaka paste on their cheeks.
MMR.history: Burma's history is a cycle of mighty kingdoms: the pagan empire built thousands of temples on the Irrawaddy plains by the 1200s, followed by the Toungoo dynasty, which created the largest empire in Southeast Asian history in the 1500s, and the Konbaung kings who fought the British. Three Anglo-Burmese wars in the 1800s ended with the last king exiled and Britain annexing Burma to British India in 1886. Independence came in 1948 after World War Two, and General Ne Win's 1962 coup began decades of isolation under the Burmese Way to Socialism. A 1988 uprising was crushed, and democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi spent years under house arrest as the military ruled. Reforms began in 2011, but a 2021 coup returned the army to power and plunged the country into civil conflict.
MMR.funFact: The Shwedagon Pagoda in Yangon is covered in real gold plates and topped with thousands of diamonds and rubies, donated over centuries.

NPL.culture: Nepali culture blends Hindu and Buddhist traditions: momo dumplings and dal bhat, Living Goddess Kumari worship in Kathmandu, and festivals like Dashain that fill the valleys with swings and kite flying. Prayer wheels and stupas mark even busy streets.
NPL.history: Nepal's Kathmandu valley hosted the sophisticated Newar kingdoms, whose artisans built pagodas that later inspired Chinese and Japanese temple design. In the late 1700s King Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha conquered the valley states and forged the modern Nepali state, whose expansion was checked by a war with British India from 1814 to 1816. The Treaty left Nepal independent but trimmed, and the British so admired the fierce Gurkha fighters that they recruited them into their army, a tradition that continues. The Shah kings lost power to hereditary Rana prime ministers for a century until a 1951 revolution restored the monarchy. A decade-long Maoist insurgency from 1996 and a 2008 vote abolished the monarchy entirely, making Nepal a secular federal republic, the world's only one with a Communist-led government born of an election.
NPL.funFact: Nepal's flag is the only national flag in the world that is not rectangular, made of two stacked triangles.

PRK.culture: North Korean culture is organized around the state: synchronized mass games with tens of thousands of performers, revolutionary operas, and shrines to the Kim dynasty. Korean traditions like kimchi and hanok-style dress survive within a system of strict control and ideological study.
PRK.history: Korea was one kingdom, Joseon, for five centuries until Japan annexed it in 1910, ruling brutally until 1945. After Japan's defeat in World War Two, the Soviet Union and the United States split the peninsula at the 38th parallel, and Kim Il-sung established a communist state in the north. His 1950 invasion of the South sparked the Korean War, which killed millions before an armistice in 1953, with no peace treaty ever signed. Kim Il-sung built a totalitarian dynasty under the Juche ideology of self-reliance, and his son Kim Jong-il and grandson Kim Jong-un inherited power, developing nuclear weapons despite isolation and sanctions. North Korea remains one of the most closed societies on Earth.
PRK.funFact: North Korea uses its own Juche calendar, which starts the year count from 1912, the birth year of Kim Il-sung.

OMN.culture: Omani culture is gentle and seafaring: frankincense perfuming souks, dates and halwa sweets with bitter kahwa coffee, and dhows still sailing from Muscat's harbors. Men wear embroidered dishdasha robes and curved khanjar daggers as symbols of pride.
OMN.history: Oman was the land of Magan, a copper supplier to Mesopotamia 4,000 years ago, and its frankincense made it wealthy when Queen of Sheba-era caravans carried the aromatic resin to Jerusalem and Rome. Omani sailors and traders spread Islam early, and the Ibadi tradition took root, unique among Muslim lands. The Portuguese seized Muscat in 1507 until Omani forces expelled them in 1650, and the Busaid dynasty, which still rules, rose in 1744. Sultan Said the Great made Oman an empire in the 1800s, ruling Zanzibar and the East African coast, making Muscat one of the richest cities in the Indian Ocean. A long communist-inspired rebellion in Dhofar ended in 1975, and Sultan Qaboos, who deposed his father in 1970, transformed Oman with oil wealth into a modern, neutral peacemaker in the Gulf.
OMN.funFact: In the 1840s the Sultan of Oman ruled territory from Muscat to Zanzibar, and at one point briefly moved his capital to the African island.

PAK.culture: Pakistani culture mixes Punjabi, Sindhi, Pashtun and Baloch traditions: qawwali Sufi music, chai and cricket on every street, and regional cuisines from karahi to chapli kebab. Colorful truck art turns every vehicle into a rolling gallery.
PAK.history: Pakistan's land hosted the Indus Valley civilization's great cities of Mohenjo-daro and Harappa over 4,000 years ago, then Gandhara's Buddhist art under Persian, Greek and Kushan rulers. Muslim sultans ruled from Delhi for centuries, and the Mughal Empire left Lahore Fort and Badshahi Mosque as masterpieces. As British India moved toward independence, Muslim leader Muhammad Ali Jinnah pushed for a separate homeland, and Pakistan was born in 1947 amid the bloody Partition that killed hundreds of thousands. It split in 1971 when East Pakistan became Bangladesh after a civil war. Pakistan has alternated between civilian and military rule, fought wars with India over Kashmir, and became a nuclear power in 1998.
PAK.funFact: Pakistan has more than 7,000 known glaciers, more than anywhere outside the polar regions, feeding the Indus River that waters the country.

famous: Jericho, one of the oldest cities
PSE.culture: Palestinian culture treasures olive harvests, tatreez embroidery patterns that identify each village, and dabke line dancing at weddings. Food like musakhan, sumac chicken over bread, and knafeh from Nablus carry deep regional pride, and poetry is a national art.
PSE.history: Palestine, the land between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean, was home to Canaanites and ancient kingdoms, and its cities like Jericho and Jerusalem are among the oldest continuously inhabited on Earth. It passed through Roman, Byzantine, Arab, Crusader and Ottoman rule, and its holiness to Jews, Christians and Muslims made it a crossroads of faiths. After the Ottoman Empire fell, Britain governed Palestine under a League of Nations Mandate and, amid rising Jewish immigration and Arab resistance, the UN voted to partition the land in 1947. The 1948 war that created Israel displaced around 700,000 Palestinians, an event called the Nakba, and the remaining territories came under Jordanian and Egyptian rule. Israel captured the West Bank and Gaza in 1967, and after the Oslo Accords of the 1990s the Palestinian Authority gained limited self-rule, while the dream of statehood remains unresolved and conflict persists.
PSE.funFact: Jericho in Palestine is often called the oldest city on Earth, with settlements dating back over 10,000 years.

PHL.culture: Filipino culture is a joyful East-meets-West mix: fiestas for every town, karaoke, basketball courts in every barangay, and dishes like adobo, sinigang and lechon. Respect for elders shows in the mano gesture, and Christmas carols start as early as September.
PHL.history: The Philippines' islands were settled by Austronesian peoples and traded with China and the Islamic world before Ferdinand Magellan arrived for Spain in 1521. Spain named the islands after King Philip II and ruled for over 300 years, converting most of the archipelago to Catholicism, the only Christian nation in Asia. Filipino rebels declared independence in 1898 as the Spanish Empire crumbled, but the United States bought the islands and crushed the new republic in a brutal war. Japan occupied the country in World War Two, and after liberation the Philippines became independent in 1946. Ferdinand Marcos's dictatorship from 1965 to 1986 was ended by the peaceful People Power revolution, a model of nonviolent change, and democracy has endured since.
PHL.funFact: Filipinos send text messages more than almost anyone on Earth, and the country is nicknamed the texting capital of the world.

famous: the world's tallest building in Doha's skyline rivals
QAT.culture: Qatari culture keeps Gulf traditions alive: falconry, dhow sailing and the majlis custom of coffee and conversation, alongside a booming arts scene in Doha's museums. Soccer fever swept the nation when it hosted the 2022 World Cup, the first in the Middle East.
QAT.history: Qatar was a pearling peninsula claimed by various Gulf powers, with the Al Thani family founding their rule in the mid-1800s after defeating local rivals. The Ottomans held nominal sway until World War One, when Britain made Qatar a protectorate in 1916. Oil discovered in 1939, and later one of the world's largest natural gas fields, turned a poor pearl coast into one of the richest nations per person. Qatar became independent in 1971 and used its gas wealth and Al Jazeera to punch far above its weight in regional politics. A blockade by neighboring states from 2017 to 2021 failed to isolate it, and the tiny emirate now hosts major world events and diplomacy.
QAT.funFact: Qatar has no permanent rivers or lakes, yet it hosted the first-ever FIFA World Cup in the Middle East with fully air-conditioned stadiums.

SAU.culture: Saudi culture is rooted in Bedouin hospitality: Arabic coffee poured from dallah pots, majlis gatherings, falconry and camel racing. Islam structures daily life, and the annual Hajj pilgrimage to Mecca draws millions of Muslims from every corner of the world.
SAU.history: The Arabian Peninsula was the birthplace of Islam in the 600s, when the Prophet Muhammad unified the tribes and the caliphs that followed spread the faith across continents. For centuries the region was a patchwork of emirates under Ottoman influence until the Saud family, allied with the reformer Ibn Abd al-Wahhab in the 1700s, began conquering the peninsula. Abdulaziz Ibn Saud captured Riyadh in 1902 and unified most of Arabia over the next three decades, founding the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932. Oil struck in 1938 turned a desert kingdom into one of the wealthiest nations on Earth and a dominant voice in world energy. Modern reforms under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman have opened cinemas, lifted driving bans on women and launched megaprojects like Neom, even as human rights debates continue.
SAU.funFact: Saudi Arabia is the birthplace of Islam and home to its two holiest cities, yet the country did not allow public cinemas until 2018.

SGP.culture: Singapore packs Malay, Chinese, Indian and Western influences into one island: hawker stalls serving laksa and Hainanese chicken rice, festivals for every faith, and strict rules that keep the garden city spotless. Kiasu, the fear of losing out, is the famous national attitude.
SGP.history: Singapore was a modest trading port called Temasek in medieval times until Britain's Stamford Raffles founded a free port there in 1819, which exploded into the crossroads of Asian trade. It became the heart of British Malaya, and Japan captured it in 1942, calling the fall of the fortress the worst disaster in British military history. After the war Singapore moved toward self-rule, and in 1963 it joined the new federation of Malaysia, but political and ethnic tensions led to its sudden, painful expulsion in 1965. Lee Kuan Yew, the founding prime minister, built a small, multiracial city-state into one of the world's wealthiest and most orderly countries within a generation. Today Singapore is a global financial hub known for efficiency, cleanliness and a mixture of democracy and paternalistic control.
SGP.funFact: Singapore banned chewing gum import and sale in 1992 after vandals stuck gum on subway door sensors, a rule only partially relaxed in 2004.

KOR.culture: South Korean culture moves fast: K-pop idol bands, binge-worthy dramas, PC bang gaming cafes, and food culture centered on kimchi, Korean barbecue and soju shared with friends. Confucian respect for elders coexists with the world's fastest high-tech society and a passion for hiking.
KOR.history: Korea's ancient kingdoms of Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla were unified by Silla in 668 AD, and the Joseon dynasty founded in 1392 ruled for five centuries, inventing the Hangul alphabet under King Sejong and earning the nickname the Hermit Kingdom. Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and ruled until 1945, when the Soviet Union and the United States divided the peninsula at the 38th parallel. North Korea's 1950 invasion sparked the Korean War, which ended in 1953 with no peace treaty and the South devastated. South Korea rose from one of the world's poorest countries to a technological powerhouse through the Miracle on the Han River, led by strongman Park Chung-hee's industrial drive. Democracy arrived after 1987's mass protests, and the Korean Wave of music, film and food has since made the country a global cultural giant.
KOR.funFact: In South Korea, babies are considered one year old at birth, and everyone gets a year older together on New Year's Day under traditional age counting.

LKA.culture: Sri Lankan culture blends Buddhist ritual with tropical abundance: rice and curry platters, kottu roti chopped on hot plates, and temple drumming during Perahera processions with decorated elephants. Cricket is a national obsession, and sari-clad women pluck tea on misty hillsides.
LKA.history: Ancient Sri Lanka, called Ceylon, built sophisticated kingdoms like Anuradhapura from the 300s BC, with vast irrigation lakes and the sacred tooth relic of the Buddha that legitimized its kings. Tamil dynasties from South India repeatedly invaded, and the rock fortress of Sigiriya, built by a parricide king around 480 AD, remains a marvel. The Portuguese arrived in 1505, followed by the Dutch and then the British, who unified the island and turned it into the world's great tea plantation, importing Tamil laborers. Independence came peacefully in 1948, but tension between the Sinhalese majority and Tamil minority exploded into a brutal 26-year civil war that ended in 2009. Sri Lanka has since rebuilt as a top tourist destination, though economic crises in recent years have tested it.
LKA.funFact: Sri Lankan kings built irrigation tanks so vast that the largest, Parakrama Samudra, is called the sea of Parakrama and is still watering rice fields today.

SYR.culture: Syrian culture is a feast of Levantine tradition: mezze of hummus and fattoush, oud music and Sufi poetry, and souks perfumed with jasmine and cardamom. Damascus is famous for jasmine-filled courtyards and artisans still weaving the legendary damask fabric.
SYR.history: Syria is one of the oldest inhabited lands on Earth, with Damascus claimed as the world's continuously inhabited capital and great trading cities like Palmyra and Ebla linking Rome, Persia and Arabia. It became a center of early Christianity and later of the Umayyad Caliphate, which ruled from Damascus an empire stretching from Spain to Central Asia in the 600s and 700s. Saladin, who fought the Crusaders, ruled from here, and later the Ottomans controlled Syria for 400 years until 1918. France took the region under a League of Nations Mandate and only left in 1946, when Syria became independent. Decades of coups brought the Assad family to power in 1970, and the civil war that erupted in 2011 devastated the country, drawing in world powers and displacing millions before the Assad regime finally fell in 2024.
SYR.funFact: Damascus steel swords were legendary for centuries, but the secret technique was lost, and modern blacksmiths still argue about how it was forged.

TWN.culture: Taiwanese culture blends Fujianese Hokkien, Hakka, indigenous and Japanese influences: night markets studded with stinky tofu and bubble tea, temple festivals with lion dances, and one of the world's friendliest, most tech-savvy societies. Convenience stores are practically national infrastructure.
TWN.history: Taiwan's Austronesian indigenous peoples lived on the island for millennia before Dutch and Spanish traders built forts in the 1600s, followed by Chinese Ming loyalist Koxinga, who expelled the Dutch in 1662. The Qing dynasty ruled Taiwan until Japan seized it in 1895 after winning a war with China. When Japan lost World War Two, the island returned to the Republic of China, but in 1949 the defeated Nationalist leader Chiang Kai-shek fled the Communist revolution and set up his government in Taipei. For decades the two Chinas each claimed to be the true government, and Taiwan democratized in the late 1980s and 1990s, holding its first direct presidential election in 1996. It grew into an economic powerhouse, producing most of the world's advanced computer chips, though its political status remains a flashpoint with Beijing.
TWN.funFact: Bubble tea was invented in Taiwan in the 1980s, and the island now produces over 90 percent of the world's most advanced semiconductor chips.

famous: ancient Silk Road cities of Panjakent
the Persian language of Central Asia
TJK.culture: Tajik culture is Persian at heart: poetry recitals honoring classical bards, plov rice feasts, and colorful chapan robes at Navruz celebrations. Mountain hospitality is legendary, and families still gather around osh shared from a single platter.
TJK.history: Tajikistan's valleys were once flourishing Silk Road hubs like Panjakent and Khujand, centers of Sogdian merchants who dominated trade between China and Europe. Persian-speaking dynasties like the Samanids made Bukhara a fountain of science and poetry in the 800s and 900s, though that capital now lies in neighboring Uzbekistan. Mongol armies under Genghis Khan swept through in the 1200s, and later Uzbek khanates ruled the Tajik lands until Russia conquered the region in the 1860s. Soviet rule in 1929 carved out Tajikistan as the only Persian-speaking Soviet republic, industrializing it but leaving it the poorest. Independence in 1991 triggered a brutal five-year civil war that killed tens of thousands, but peace returned and Tajikistan has since become known for its dramatic mountains and hydropower.
TJK.funFact: Over 90 percent of Tajikistan is mountainous, and the Pamir Highway is one of the highest roads in the world, passing passes above 4,600 meters.

THA.culture: Thai culture glows with the golden temples and floating markets, the polite wai greeting, and the spicy-sweet balance of tom yum and pad thai. The monarchy is deeply revered, Muay Thai matches draw village crowds, and the Buddhist new year of Songkran turns streets into water fights.
THA.history: Thailand grew out of kingdoms like Sukhothai, founded in 1238, and Ayutthaya, whose capital was one of the world's grandest cities until Burma burned it in 1767. The Chakri dynasty, which still reigns, moved the capital to Bangkok, and King Mongkut and Chulalongkorn modernized Siam in the 1800s while playing Britain and France off against each other. That diplomacy made Siam the only Southeast Asian country never colonized by a European power. A 1932 revolution ended absolute monarchy, and the country allied with Japan in World War Two, then became a US partner during the Vietnam era while alternating between military coups and elected governments. Thailand has since become a tourism powerhouse, famous for beaches, street food and temples, despite ongoing political turbulence.
THA.funFact: Thailand's capital has the world's longest ceremonial name, over 160 letters, which most Thais shorten to the single word Krung Thep, meaning city of angels.

TLS.culture: Timorese culture blends indigenous traditions with Portuguese colonial and Catholic heritage: tais woven cloth patterns, church festivals alongside animist rituals, and coffee grown on steep green mountains. Food staples include rice, corn and ikan sabuko grilled fish with spicy sambal.
TLS.history: Timor island was a Portuguese trading post from the 1500s, prized for sandalwood, with the western half becoming Dutch, a split that survives today as the border with Indonesia. Portugal neglected the colony until the 1974 revolution in Lisbon opened the door to decolonization, and East Timor declared independence in 1975. Nine days later Indonesia invaded and annexed the territory, beginning an occupation marked by famine and violence that killed a large share of the population. Resistance led by figures like Xanana Gusmao and the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize for Bishop Belo and Jose Ramos-Horta kept the cause alive. A UN-backed referendum in 1999 chose independence, and after violent reprisals by militias, Timor-Leste finally became Asia's newest country in 2002.
TLS.funFact: Timor-Leste was the first new sovereign nation of the 21st century, and its inhabitants were among the first humans to reach the region, over 40,000 years ago.

TUR.culture: Turkish culture is a bridge of tastes and sounds: kebabs and simit tea breaks, the whirling ceremonies of the Mevlevi dervishes, and bazaars piled with carpets and spices. Family tables stretch for hours, and football, backgammon and cay drinking fill the day.
TUR.history: Anatolia hosted the Hittites, Troy of Greek legend, and Byzantium, whose capital Constantinople was the center of the Christian world for a thousand years. Turkic peoples arrived in the 1000s, and the Seljuks and then the Ottomans rose, with Mehmed the Conqueror capturing Constantinople in 1453 and ending the Roman Empire's last chapter. The Ottoman Empire then ruled the Balkans, Middle East and North Africa for over 400 years, reaching its peak under Suleiman the Magnificent. Defeat in World War One dismembered the empire, and Mustafa Kemal Ataturk led a war of independence, founding the Republic of Turkiye in 1923 and remaking it as a secular modern nation. Turkey joined NATO in 1952, grew into a major regional power, and now balances between Europe, the Middle East and the former Ottoman world.
TUR.funFact: Turkey has more ancient Greek ruins than Greece in some categories, and Saint Nicholas, the real Santa Claus, was born on its southern coast.

famous: the Gates of Hell gas crater
TKM.culture: Turkmen culture is nomadic and tribal: hand-woven carpets with tribal motifs, Akhal-Teke golden horses, and the melancholy dutar lute. Traditions of hospitality, melon festivals and old silk road songs survive beneath a very controlled modern state.
TKM.history: Turkmen lands were crossed by Silk Road caravans between Merv, once one of the world's largest cities, and the Caspian, and were ruled by Persians, Arabs, Seljuks and Mongols. The Oghuz Turkic tribes that settled here became the Turkmen, whose cavalry under the Seljuk sultans built an empire stretching to the Mediterranean. In the 1800s Russia conquered the Turkmen steppe after fierce resistance at the Battle of Geok Tepe, and the Soviets incorporated the land in 1924. Independence in 1991 brought the eccentric rule of Saparmurat Niyazov, who styled himself Turkmenbashi, father of the Turkmen, renamed the months and built a rotating golden statue of himself. His successor opened the economy slightly, and Turkmenistan remains one of the most isolated countries on Earth, sitting on vast natural gas reserves.
TKM.funFact: Turkmenistan's Darvaza gas crater has been burning since 1971, nicknamed the Gates of Hell, and officials have tried to figure out how to extinguish it for years.

ARE.culture: Emirati culture keeps Bedouin traditions alive: falconry, camel racing with robot jockeys, and Majlis hospitality over Arabic coffee and dates. Skyscrapers and souks sit side by side, and Friday after prayers, families gather for machboos rice feasts.
ARE.history: The UAE's coast was ancient Magan, a pearling and copper land, and its ports traded with Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley 4,000 years ago. In the 1700s and 1800s the area became known as the Pirate Coast to the British, who signed peace treaties with the local sheikhdoms and turned them into the Trucial States, a loose protectorate. Oil discovered in Abu Dhabi in 1958 changed everything, transforming fishing villages into gleaming cities within a generation. When Britain withdrew from the Gulf, seven emirates united on December 2, 1971 to form the United Arab Emirates, with Abu Dhabi and Dubai as powerhouses. Under rulers like Sheikh Zayed, the federation became a global aviation, trade and tourism hub, home to the world's tallest building.
ARE.funFact: The Burj Khalifa in Dubai is so tall that people on the ground floor break their fast during Ramadan about two minutes before those on the top floor.

famous: Silk Road cities of Bukhara and Khiva
UZB.culture: Uzbek culture is the soul of the Silk Road: plov cooked by master chefs in giant cauldrons, suzani embroidery, and the maqom classical music tradition. Hospitality is sacred, guests are blessed, and bazaars overflow with spices, melons and handmade ceramics.
UZB.history: Uzbekistan's oasis cities were the crown jewels of the Silk Road, where Timur, known in the West as Tamerlane, built an empire from Samarkand in the late 1300s and filled it with turquoise domes and captured artisans. His descendants, the Timurids, fostered a golden age of astronomy and mathematics, and the astronomer Ulugh Beg mapped the stars from Samarkand. Uzbek tribes swept in from the north in the 1500s, founding the khanates of Bukhara, Khiva and Kokand that ruled until Russia absorbed the region in the 1860s and 1870s. Soviet rule carved out the Uzbek republic in 1924, cotton monoculture devastated the land and the Aral Sea shrank to near nothing. Independence in 1991 under Islam Karimov brought strict authoritarian rule, and after his death in 2016 the country has slowly opened up, welcoming travelers to its restored Silk Road cities.
UZB.funFact: Samarkand's bread is so beloved that Uzbeks joke you can take it anywhere in the world and it will taste of home, and travelers still carry round loaves home from visits.

VNM.culture: Vietnamese culture blends rice paddies and street food, family ancestor altars and Tet new year celebrations when the whole country travels home. Confucian respect for learning, Buddhist temples, and French colonial cafe culture mix in daily life, and pho is eaten morning, noon and night.
VNM.history: Vietnam began with the Red River delta kingdoms and was ruled by China for a thousand years, winning independence in 938 AD after the battle on the Bach Dang River. The Ly, Tran and later Le dynasties built a Confucian state, pushed south to conquer the Champa kingdom and the Mekong delta, and repelled Mongol invasions three times. France seized Vietnam in the mid-1800s, joining it into colonial Indochina, and Japanese occupation during World War Two opened the door to Ho Chi Minh's declaration of independence in 1945. The First Indochina War ended French rule at Dien Bien Phu in 1954, but the country split in two and the Vietnam War raged until 1975, when communist North Vietnam reunified the country after American withdrawal. Since economic reforms launched in 1986, Vietnam has transformed into one of Asia's fastest-growing economies.
VNM.funFact: Vietnam is the world's second-largest coffee exporter and invented its own drink, ca phe sua da, iced coffee with sweetened condensed milk.

YEM.culture: Yemeni culture is ancient and tribal: qat chewing afternoons, honey considered the best in the world, and jambiya curved daggers worn by men. The mudbrick tower houses of the old cities and the terraced highlands give the country its unmistakable look.
YEM.history: Yemen was the land of Saba, the biblical Sheba, whose Queen supposedly visited King Solomon, and whose legendary Marib dam made the desert bloom for a thousand years before it collapsed around 570 AD. The frankincense and myrrh trade made the region fabulously wealthy, and Yemeni ports connected the Roman, Persian and Indian worlds. Coffee was first brewed here in the 1400s, and the port of Mocha gave its name to the drink itself. The Ottoman Empire and later imams of the Zaidi dynasty ruled the highlands until North Yemen became independent in 1918, while the British held Aden in the south until 1967. The two Yemens united in 1990, but civil wars, an Arab Spring uprising, and the devastating conflict that began in 2014 between the Houthi movement and a Saudi-backed government have created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
YEM.funFact: Yemeni Sufi monks were the first to brew coffee as we know it in the 1400s, and every cup of coffee in the world descends from plants smuggled out of Yemen.
